reference.source: Standard endocrinology texts and congenital hypothyroidism guidance
clinicalPearls: A cause of congenital hypothyroidism in which the thyroid gland is present, often enlarged (goitre), but cannot make hormone normally
Usually autosomal recessive, arising from defects in steps of hormone synthesis such as iodide transport, organification (thyroid peroxidase), thyroglobulin, or hydrogen peroxide generation (DUOX2)
Detected in many countries through newborn screening showing a raised thyroid-stimulating hormone
Distinguished from thyroid dysgenesis by the presence of a normally sited or enlarged gland on imaging
Pendred syndrome combines an organification defect with sensorineural hearing loss, so hearing should be assessed
A perchlorate discharge test can demonstrate an organification defect where such testing is available
Prompt levothyroxine replacement started in the neonatal period prevents the neurodevelopmental consequences of untreated congenital hypothyroidism
reference.pathophysiology: Thyroid dyshormonogenesis is caused by inherited defects in the enzymatic machinery the thyroid uses to synthesise hormone. Depending on the gene involved, iodide may not be trapped or organified, thyroglobulin may be abnormal, or the hydrogen peroxide needed for organification may be deficient. Impaired hormone output lowers circulating thyroid hormone and, through loss of negative feedback, raises thyroid-stimulating hormone. The resulting chronic stimulation causes the gland to enlarge into a goitre, while the hormone deficiency itself threatens growth and, critically in infancy, neurodevelopment.
additionalDifferentials: Transient neonatal hypothyroidism from maternal or iodine factors
Maternal antithyroid drug or antibody effects
additionalInvestigations: Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine
Thyroid ultrasound to confirm a present or enlarged gland
Radionuclide uptake scan to assess trapping and gland location
Perchlorate discharge test for organification defects
Serum and urine thyroglobulin and iodine studies
Genetic testing of relevant synthesis genes and audiology for suspected Pendred syndrome
redFlags: Delayed recognition or treatment in a neonate risking irreversible neurodevelopmental impairment
A rapidly enlarging or compressive goitre
Associated sensorineural hearing loss suggesting Pendred syndrome
Severe hypothyroid features such as feeding difficulty and hypotonia in infancy
reference.prognosis: When congenital hypothyroidism is detected by screening and treated promptly with adequate replacement, growth and neurodevelopment are usually normal; delayed treatment risks permanent cognitive impairment, and the goitre generally regresses once hormone levels are restored.
pitfalls: Assuming a present gland excludes a hormone synthesis defect
Missing associated deafness in Pendred syndrome
Delaying replacement while awaiting confirmatory imaging or genetics in a neonate
Under-dosing replacement and allowing persistent goitre or hypothyroidism
references: European Society for Paediatric Endocrinology congenital hypothyroidism guidance
management: Start prompt, lifelong levothyroxine replacement titrated to restore euthyroidism as soon as congenital hypothyroidism is confirmed on newborn screening
Titrate the levothyroxine dose against thyroid function and clinical response, ensuring adequate replacement through infancy to protect neurodevelopment
Monitor growth, developmental milestones and thyroid function at regular intervals, expecting the goitre to regress once hormone levels are restored
Assess hearing with audiology where Pendred syndrome is suspected, and provide aural rehabilitation for sensorineural hearing loss
Adjust replacement during intercurrent illness, growth and puberty to avoid under-treatment
Offer genetic counselling and family screening, as the disorder is usually autosomal recessive
Refer to paediatric endocrinology and clinical genetics for coordinated care
